title: Formal Acceleration on FPGA. Innovation in Verification - Semiwiki
gist: Bernard Murphy, with Cadence's Paul Cunningham and Silicon Catalyst's Raul Camposano, reviews UCLA's SAT-Accel paper: an FPGA SAT solver reaching 800x over the prior FPGA state of the art but only 2.8-3x over Kissat on a 64-core AMD Epyc, capped at 32k variables and 131k clauses by on-chip SRAM while industrial EDA instances run to tens of millions of variables.

themes.theme: Hardware acceleration reaches an unaccelerated verification domain

insights.claim: Formal verification is a verification domain that has not received much attention for hardware acceleration, making SAT acceleration a comparatively open research area.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: White space in EDA acceleration; emulation and simulation acceleration are crowded, formal is not.
insights.quote: a verification domain that has not got much attention for acceleration
insights.locator: Extending hardware acceleration to formal verification

insights.claim: SAT is arguably the algorithm most fundamental to verification, lying at the heart of both formal verification and constrained random stimulus generation.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Any durable SAT speedup would compound across a large share of EDA verification workloads and compute spend.
insights.quote: It is hard to pick an algorithm more fundamental to verification than SAT

insights.claim: SAT is NP-complete yet many practical algorithms have been developed, and it is widely used in EDA applications including equivalence checking, bounded model checking, ATPG and logic optimization.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Maps the specific EDA product lines whose runtimes a SAT breakthrough would touch.

insights.claim: CPU-based SAT solvers have advanced on many fronts over the years without noticeably taking advantage of hardware acceleration, leaving a structural gap this work targets.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Frames why FPGA SAT is a credible research direction rather than a solved problem.
insights.locator: CPU-based SAT solvers have advanced on many fronts

themes.theme: SAT-Accel results and where they come from

insights.claim: SAT-Accel achieves an 800x speed-up over SAT-Hard, the best previous FPGA-based SAT solver, because prior FPGA SAT work neglected the modern solver strategies that deliver orders-of-magnitude speedups on real-world use cases.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: The headline number is measured against a weak FPGA baseline, not against production software, so discount it accordingly.
insights.quote: achieves 800x speed-up over the best previous FPGA-based SAT solver, SAT-Hard

insights.claim: Against software, SAT-Accel is 17.9x faster than MiniSat but only 2.8x faster than Kissat, and averages roughly a 3x speed-up versus Kissat running on a 64-core AMD Epyc.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: A roughly 3x edge over state-of-the-art CPU software is far below the threshold that would justify displacing CPU verification farms.
insights.quote: it is 17.9x faster than MiniSat and 2.8x faster than Kissat

insights.claim: Benchmarks that could not fit into the FPGA's on-chip memory were excluded from the comparison, meaning the reported software-relative speedups are measured only on the subset of problems the accelerator can hold.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: A selection-bias caveat that materially weakens the benchmark claim; the standard diligence question for any accelerator paper.
insights.quote: Benchmarks that could not fit into the FPGA’s on-chip memory were excluded from the comparison.

insights.claim: SAT-Accel's architecture comprises a specialized memory access unit, an array of processing elements to parallelize propagating variable assignments through the expression, and a dedicated unit performing on-the-fly clause minimization and search rollback.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: The architectural template for domain-specific SAT hardware that others may copy or license.

insights.claim: SAT-Accel implements Conflict-Driven Clause Learning, Clause Minimization, Clause Deletion, Solver Restart Policy, Phase Saving, Variable Decision Heuristics and Efficient Clause Checking, while omitting Kissat heuristics such as advanced phase selection, chronological backtracking, and variable and clause elimination.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: The omitted heuristics are where remaining CPU advantage lives, and where the gap could widen or close.

insights.claim: SAT solving is memory-bound rather than compute-bound: variables are accessed in irregular order, execution is memory-latency bound, and cache misses dominate runtime while arithmetic units remain mostly idle.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Explains why throughput-oriented accelerators are poorly matched to SAT and why memory architecture is the real design lever.
insights.locator: Perhaps the most interesting aspect of the work

insights.claim: The authors introduce a page-based memory manager whose pages can be immediately recycled without compaction, and maintain two representations of the SAT instance, a clause-oriented one for learning and minimization and a transposed variable-oriented one for propagation.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: The transferable technical idea is trading storage for latency, applicable beyond SAT to other irregular-access accelerators.
insights.locator: To address this, the authors introduce a page-based memory manager

insights.claim: Maintaining two specialized memory organizations increases storage requirements but significantly reduces memory access latency, largely eliminating the memory bottleneck at the cost of tighter capacity limits.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: The design's core tradeoff, and the direct cause of its capacity ceiling.
insights.locator: Maintaining two specialized memory organizations increases storage requirements

insights.claim: SAT-Accel works only with SRAM on the FPGA, limiting it to 32k variables and 131k clauses, with the FPGA's roughly 107 MB of on-chip memory on the U55C constraining problem size.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: The hard capacity number that determines whether this is a lab result or a product.
insights.quote: SAT-Accel works only with SRAM on the FPGA, which limits it to 32k variables and 131k clauses.
insights.locator: It’s main challenge and the authors’ focus

insights.claim: To be of commercial value, SAT capacity needs to reach millions of variables and clauses, requiring either off-chip DRAM with some form of caching scheme or distribution of the solver across multiple FPGAs.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Names the two engineering paths that would turn this into a commercial EDA accelerator; watch for follow-up work taking either.
insights.quote: To be of commercial value, capacity needs to be in the millions of variables and clauses.

insights.claim: Verifying a design with 500,000 flip-flops, 5 million logic gates and 200 clock cycles of unrolling can easily produce Boolean formulas with tens of millions of variables, roughly three orders of magnitude beyond the accelerator's 32k-variable ceiling.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Quantifies the gap between the accelerator and real industrial verification workloads.
insights.locator: For example, verifying a design with 500,000 flip-flops

insights.claim: SAT-Accel is a compelling architectural proof of concept for domain-specific acceleration in niches whose problems fit its fixed memory footprint, such as the quantum compilation benchmarks the authors highlight.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: The near-term addressable use case is quantum compilation rather than mainstream EDA verification.
insights.locator: In summary, SAT-Accel is a compelling architectural proof of concept

insights.claim: For the multi-million-variable SAT instances common in industrial EDA, software solvers implementing Kissat-like algorithms on CPUs remain the practical solution.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: A near-term negative call on FPGA formal acceleration disrupting CPU-based verification compute demand.
insights.quote: software solvers implementing Kissat-like algorithms on CPUs remain the practical solution
insights.locator: However, for the multi-million-variable SAT instances
